abstract: Agentic AI systems retrieve institutional records, retain memory, invoke tools, delegate to other agents, and initiate actions that change what an institution holds about a person. The assurance question they raise is no longer whether a model answers correctly, but what it can cause when it is mistaken, manipulated, or pursuing an objective it has not disclosed. Trust by Construction answers that question architecturally. The model is treated as an untrusted reasoning engine rather than as a security boundary, and the same rule is extended to any model that reviews another, so that authorisation depends on neither the acting nor the reviewing model's judgment. Authority is declared in machine-readable form, narrowed to a single task, attenuated across delegation, and enforced by deterministic services that sit outside the reasoning layer. The contribution is the composition and its behaviour under failure: scoped capability leases, lineage-preserving memory, independent approval, revocation that survives failure of the assurance plane itself, delivery reauthorised at every boundary, restrict-only monitoring that can never return privilege, bounded recovery from effects that leave the transaction, and accounting for the information an agent can carry in choices it is authorised to make. The architecture is published as an executable Apache-2.0 kernel in which every claim is bound to a named failure test and every reported quantity regenerates offline, so a reader can run the refusals rather than accept them on trust. The design rule is proof before power: additional context, tools, agents, network reach, effects, and releases each require independently verifiable authority. The paper reports what this establishes and what it does not — behaviour within declared interfaces, not model alignment, decision quality, institutional outcomes, or production security — and names the deployment obligations that remain.
notes: v15 is a presentation and scholarship revision. It removes revision-diary framing so the manuscript reads as a first submission, rewrites the abstract to lead with the problem and the contribution, states the central claim as a named property, credits the capability, information-flow and confinement results the architecture restates, names the governance frameworks the education argument answers to, and adds a reading guide, a terminology table, a related-work placement table and an extension recipe. No claim, quantity, control or limitation is added, removed or weakened. The evidence scope is stated once where it belongs rather than repeated in every table row and caption; the limitations section is unchanged.

contributions: This paper makes four contributions. First, a composition: the authority controls above are specified as one enforcement path from workload declaration through context, memory, delegation and effects to recipient delivery, with the behaviour of each under failure stated as a refusal rather than as a best effort. Second, a falsifiable central claim. That authorisation depends on neither the acting nor the reviewing model is tested by substituting a monitor that clears every attack and a monitor that restricts every ordinary task, and showing that no protected outcome changes under either. Third, a measured account of a channel that content controls cannot close: the information an agent carries in the destination, path, timing, size and number of releases it is authorised to make, reduced from sixteen bits to one and then to zero by removing choice rather than by inspecting content, with the availability cost of doing so reported alongside. Fourth, an executable artifact in which every claim made here names a failure test that runs offline, every reported quantity regenerates from its source, and the manuscript itself is produced by a script from reviewed content so that each change to its prose is reviewable as code.
results_summary: Four results carry the argument, and each is reported with its denominator and its boundary. Removing any one of the eight tested controls re-enables a harmful action, so none of them is decorative. Across six sector profiles the mediated configuration contains every hostile scenario in the corpus while completing every benign task. Substituting a blind monitor, and then a hostile monitor that inverts every verdict, changes no protected outcome, which is the falsifiable form of the central claim. And an adversary restricted to choices it is authorised to make moves a sixteen-bit secret intact through an unconstrained release path, one bit once those choices are canonicalised, and nothing once the number of releases is fixed. Table 3 states what each measurement does and does not establish.

property_statement: Property 1 (Authorisation independence). For every protected read, effect and release, the outcome is a function of the declared authority state alone — passport, task contract, capability envelope, lineage and remaining budget — and not of any text produced by the acting model or by a model reviewing it. A model may narrow an outcome and may cause a refusal; it cannot cause an outcome that the authority state does not already permit. Stated this way the property is falsifiable in the strong sense, because refuting it requires only one protected outcome that changes when the reasoning or reviewing model's output changes while the authority state is held fixed. Section 4 reports the attempt to refute it. The formulation is the complete-mediation and least-privilege pair [13] applied to a component that is assumed to be untrustworthy rather than merely faulty, and the one-directional monitor that follows from it is the integrity discipline of [18]: a lower-integrity source may restrict a higher-integrity decision and may never raise one.
reading_guide: How to read this paper. Section 2 states the architecture and the property it targets; sections 3 to 8 report what was built and what happened when that property was attacked; sections 9 and 10 state where the result applies and where it does not. A reader with ten minutes should read Property 1 in section 2, Table 3 in section 4, and section 10, in that order, because those three together contain the claim, the evidence and the boundary. Seven terms carry most of the argument and are used in exactly one sense throughout.

extension_recipe: Extending the kernel follows the path the kernel itself took, and is deliberately short. A new domain is a profile: declare its resources, purposes, destinations and permitted effects, and the existing conformance suite runs against it unchanged, which is how the six sector packs were produced from the first. A new control is a capability contract: name the protected asset, the permitted operation, the enforcement point, the accountable owner, the failure test, the evidence artifact and the failure response, and the verifier executes the named test and refuses to count a contract whose test does not run. A new written claim is an entry in the claim register binding that sentence to that test, so a claim whose evidence is later removed fails the build instead of surviving into print. A new threat is a falsifier: express it as an attempt to produce a protected outcome the authority state forbids, and add it to the bounded search. None of these four requires modifying the enforcement core, which is the precise sense in which the architecture is extensible: the core stays small and auditable while the declarations grow.
threat_model: Threat model. The adversary is assumed to control everything the reasoning layer produces and everything it reads: model outputs, retrieved documents, memory written in earlier turns, tool descriptions and tool results, messages from delegated agents, and the verdict of any model deployed to monitor another. It may choose freely among the operations it has been granted, may repeat them, and may time them. It is assumed not to control the enforcement path itself — the control database, the operator role, the signing keys, and the host outside the declared interfaces — because an adversary holding those has already won and no architecture recovers from it. That assumption is a deployment obligation, and section 8 measures it rather than asserting it. Every property below is stated relative to this model, so a deployment that cannot establish the assumption inherits a weaker claim than the one made here.
